title: A Synapse Made of a Channel

scenes.tts: A mouse taste cell can detect sweet, bitter or umami. But this cell has no conventional vesicular synapse. So how does the news reach the nerve fibre? Everything in this film is a mouse result. None of it is a human map.
scenes.visual: A taste cell and a nerve fibre with an empty gap; vesicles crossed out; a question mark fills the gap.
scenes.narration: A mouse taste cell can detect sweet, bitter or umami. But this cell has no conventional vesicular synapse. So how does the news reach the nerve fibre? Everything in this film is a mouse result. None of it is a human map.

scenes.tts: These are type two taste cells. They carry the receptors for sweet, bitter and umami. Those are G protein coupled receptors. When the cell is depolarized, it releases A T P through a channel. The nerve fibre beside it carries an A T P receptor.
scenes.caption: These are type II taste cells. They carry the receptors for sweet, bitter and umami. Those are G protein coupled receptors. When the cell is depolarized, it releases ATP through a channel. The nerve fibre beside it carries an ATP receptor.
scenes.visual: Receptor chips light up; a channel appears in the cell membrane; ATP chips pass through it to the receptor on the fibre.
scenes.narration: These are type II taste cells. They carry the receptors for sweet, bitter and umami. Those are G protein coupled receptors. When the cell is depolarized, it releases ATP through a channel. The nerve fibre beside it carries an ATP receptor.

scenes.tts: Tah-roo-no and colleagues found that C A L H M one is required for taste-evoked A T P release from mouse type two cells. They used knockout mice, isolated cells, taste tissue, nerve recordings and behaviour. Without that channel, the release fails. Sour and salty recognition was mostly normal in the assays they tested. For sour, that fits release at a vesicular synapse. That does not mean that sodium signalling never uses C A L H M channels.
scenes.caption: Taruno and colleagues found that CALHM1 is required for taste-evoked ATP release from mouse type II cells. They used knockout mice, isolated cells, taste tissue, nerve recordings and behaviour. Without that channel, the release fails. Sour and salty recognition was mostly normal in the assays they tested. For sour, that fits release at a vesicular synapse. That does not mean that sodium signalling never uses CALHM channels.
scenes.visual: The channel is named CALHM1. In the knockout case the channel is gone and the ATP stays inside.
scenes.narration: Taruno and colleagues found that CALHM1 is required for taste-evoked ATP release from mouse type II cells. They used knockout mice, isolated cells, taste tissue, nerve recordings and behaviour. Without that channel, the release fails. Sour and salty recognition was mostly normal in the assays they tested. For sour, that fits release at a vesicular synapse. That does not mean that sodium signalling never uses CALHM channels.

scenes.tts: A puzzle remained. C A L H M one alone is slow. In mouse N two A cells, recorded by whole-cell voltage clamp, it activated with a time constant above five hundred milliseconds. Voltage clamp holds the membrane potential fixed while the channel currents are recorded.
scenes.caption: A puzzle remained. CALHM1 alone is slow. In mouse N2a cells, recorded by whole-cell voltage clamp, it activated with a time constant above 500 milliseconds. Voltage clamp holds the membrane potential fixed while the channel currents are recorded.
scenes.visual: Membrane bar with a CALHM1 chip; a slow rising activation curve with a 500 ms time constant, labelled in this sketch.
scenes.narration: A puzzle remained. CALHM1 alone is slow. In mouse N2a cells, recorded by whole-cell voltage clamp, it activated with a time constant above 500 milliseconds. Voltage clamp holds the membrane potential fixed while the channel currents are recorded.

scenes.tts: Ma and colleagues deleted C. A. L. H. M. three in mice. Taste-evoked A T P release from taste buds was abolished. In the cultured cells, C. A. L. H. M. one with C. A. L. H. M. three activated in about ten milliseconds. That is a speed-up of more than fifty-fold. The authors concluded that C. A. L. H. M. three supplies the rapid gating that a C. A. L. H. M. one only account lacked.
scenes.caption: Ma and colleagues deleted Calhm3 in mice. Taste-evoked ATP release from taste buds was abolished. In the cultured cells, CALHM1 with CALHM3 activated in about 10 milliseconds. That is a speed-up of more than fifty-fold. The authors concluded that Calhm3 supplies the rapid gating that a CALHM1-only account lacked.
scenes.visual: Deletion case with release abolished is cleared; CALHM3 joins CALHM1 on the membrane; a much steeper curve appears; 500 over 10.
scenes.narration: Ma and colleagues deleted Calhm3 in mice. Taste-evoked ATP release from taste buds was abolished. In the cultured cells, CALHM1 with CALHM3 activated in about 10 milliseconds. That is a speed-up of more than fifty-fold. The authors concluded that Calhm3 supplies the rapid gating that a CALHM1-only account lacked.

scenes.tts: Keep the limits in mind. The exact times depend on voltage and protocol. They are properties of cultured cells, not delays measured in a living animal. So here is the rule to keep. In mouse type two taste cells, A T P leaves through C. A. L. H. M. channels, and C. A. L. H. M. three speeds the gating.
